title: The GGM Construction: PRGs Make PRFs

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 2.7-2.8 (GGM construction; stronger notions; conceptual reflections).

body:
## From one long string to an exponential table

A pseudorandom generator produces one long pseudorandom string from one short seed — but the consumer must read the string, or at least generate it in full. Many settings instead need **random access to the bits of a huge pseudorandom sequence**: think of associating a random-looking value with each of exponentially many possible messages, tags, or addresses, where the relevant values are only discovered online and cannot be enumerated or stored in advance. The tool that provides this is a **pseudorandom function (PRF)**: a seed $s$ of length $k$ defines a function $f_s : \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$ that is *efficiently computable at every point* and yet is indistinguishable, to anyone holding only an oracle, from a truly random function $F : \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$.

@def:prf17

Three structural facts worth internalizing:

- **An exponential object with a tiny program.** An explicit table of a random function $\{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$ has $2^k$ entries of $k$ bits — $k \cdot 2^k$ bits in total. The seed $s$ is a $k$-bit program for that whole table (together with the shared evaluation algorithm).
- **Oracle-only access.** The distinguisher never receives the seed or any description of $f_s$; it learns only the answers to the queries it makes. The definition must capture testing a black box, not inspecting code.
- **Full adversarial freedom in the queries.** The oracle machine is probabilistic polynomial-time, may query any points (even adaptively, each query depending on previous answers), and yet outputs a single bit. Both features are essential and are discussed in Exercise m5ggm-ex-3 below.

**Why sharing a seed is sharing a function.** If two parties share $s$, they both can compute $f_s$ — and so they can agree, *without further communication and without synchronization*, on a random-looking value $f_s(v)$ for any $v$ that arises online. This "shared randomness on demand" is the engine behind message authentication and private-key encryption schemes built from pseudorandom functions, and PRFs are also the pivot of negative results in computational learning theory and of the Natural Proofs framework in circuit complexity (see "Why this matters" at the end).

## Warm-up: how strong must the generator be? (recap of §2.6 and §2.7.1)

Before building PRFs, recall why the *plain* PRG definition was not enough for worst-case derandomization. Replacing the random tape of a BPP algorithm by $G(U_k)$ only guarantees that no *efficiently findable* input is affected (an average-case statement). To derandomize a class such as BPP in the worst case, the generator must fool **all** polynomial-size circuits — a non-uniform guarantee — because each potentially bad input gets hard-wired into a circuit that tests the generator (this is the source of non-uniformity in the proof of Theorem 2.16 below).

@def:strong-generators

The point of quantifying resources as a function of the **seed length $k$** (rather than of the output length $\ell(k)$) is that the adversary is then parameterized exactly the way derandomization needs: a single seed length controls both the generator's output and the resources of everything it must fool. As motivation/contrast, recall the derandomization consequence that non-uniformly strong generators yield:

@thm:thm216

**Reading Theorem 2.16.** The proof replaces the $n$-bit random tape of a BPP procedure $A$ by $G(U_{n^\varepsilon})$ and then scans all $2^{n^\varepsilon}$ seeds, ruling by majority. Each input $x$ on which the randomized and the pseudorandom versions diverge yields the circuit $C_x(r) = A(x; r)$, a poly-size circuit that distinguishes $G(U_{n^\varepsilon})$ from $U_{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ — contradicting Definition 2.15; hence only finitely many such inputs exist, and they can be absorbed into the algorithm. This gives deterministic time $2^{n^\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. The familiar slogan "randomness in BPP can be eliminated (essentially at polynomial cost)" becomes literally $\mathrm{BPP} \subseteq \mathrm{P}$ only when generators with exponential stretch exist (seed length $O(\log n)$, so scanning all seeds costs $\mathrm{poly}(n)$) — this is the subject of Chapter 3 (Module 6). Section 2.7.1 also warns that the Chapter-2 construction route (Theorem 2.14, one-way functions) yields only much weaker $(T',F')$-strong generators with $t'(k) = t(k^\varepsilon)/\mathrm{poly}(k)$ for a fixed $\varepsilon = 1/8$ — far from the desired $t(\ell(k))/\mathrm{poly}(k)$. Building very strong generators is genuinely harder and will force the paradigm flip of Chapter 3, where the generator is allowed to be *slower* than the distinguishers it fools.

## The GGM construction: grow a function out of a generator

We now prove that **any** PRG — no further assumptions — yields a PRF. This is Theorem 2.18 of the Primer (Goldreich, Goldwasser, Micali). Assume $G$ is a PRG with stretch factor exactly 2: it maps $k$-bit seeds to $2k$-bit strings, which we split into two halves

$$G(s) = G_0(s) \, G_1(s), \qquad |G_0(s)| = |G_1(s)| = |s| = k.$$

(Any PRG with stretch $\ell(k) \ge k+1$ can first be amplified to stretch $2k$ via Construction 2.7, so this normalization loses nothing.) Think of $G_0$ and $G_1$ as two "child generators": from any string $r$ we can produce two fresh $|r|$-bit strings $G_0(r)$ and $G_1(r)$.

@def:ggm-tree

**Cost analysis.** Evaluating $f_s(x)$ walks down exactly $k$ edges, and each edge costs one evaluation of $G$: to move from a node labeled $r$ to its left (resp. right) child we run $G(r)$ once and keep $G_0(r)$ (resp. $G_1(r)$). So $f_s(x)$ costs **$k$ applications of $G$**, never $2^k$: the other $2^{k+1}-2$ tree vertices are never materialized. Since $G$ is polynomial-time, $f_s$ is computable in polynomial time (in $|s| = |x| = k$), as required by condition 1 of Definition 2.17. Note also that every vertex at level $i \le k$ carries a label of length $k$ (halves stay length $k$), so the construction is well defined all the way to the leaves, which carry the $k$-bit outputs.

The intuition: the seed $s$ is a random "origin", and each application of $G$ unfolds fresh pseudorandom material. The tree is the branching program of the function — input bits steer a root-to-leaf walk, and the PRG generates exactly the labels on the walked path. The security claim is that the $2^k$ leaf labels "look like" $2^k$ independent random $k$-bit strings to any efficient oracle machine.

## Theorem 2.18: PRG ⇒ PRF

@thm:ggm

**Why this is surprising.** A PRG produces only $\ell(k)$ bits from $k$ bits, but $f_s$ must present $2^k$ values that jointly look random. The tree is the bridge: it *recycles* pseudorandomness — each level-$i$ label is used to generate two level-$(i+1)$ labels, so the $2^i$ labels at level $i$ "unfold" into $2^{i+1}$ labels at level $i+1$. The challenge is to prove that this massive reuse does not create detectable structure; the proof peels the tree one level at a time and charges every peeling step to the PRG property.

## Anatomy of the hybrid proof (details completed)

The proof is a hybrid argument over the tree levels, and it is worth completing every step carefully, since the reduction has a subtle quantitative structure.

**Step 1 — define the hybrids.** For $i = 0, 1, \ldots, k$, the $i$-th hybrid $\mathcal{H}_k^i$ is an ensemble of functions $\{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$, each determined by a tuple $\bar{s} = \langle s_\sigma \rangle_{\sigma \in \{0,1\}^i}$ of $2^i$ independent uniform $k$-bit strings (one per vertex of level $i$). Pictorially: **place the random strings at the level-$i$ vertices, and label every vertex *below* level $i$ by the deterministic GGM rule** (left child $G_0(r)$, right child $G_1(r)$ of a node labeled $r$). Formally, writing an input as $x = \sigma \alpha$ with $|\sigma| = i$ and $|\alpha| = k - i$, the value is the label obtained by starting at the level-$i$ vertex $\sigma$ (labeled $s_\sigma$) and walking down along $\alpha$ by the GGM rule:

$$h_{\bar{s}}(\sigma\alpha) = G_{\alpha_{k-i}}\!\big(\cdots G_{\alpha_2}\big(G_{\alpha_1}(s_\sigma)\big)\cdots\big).$$

**Step 2 — the extremes are exactly what we need.** At $i = 0$ there is a single random string placed at level 0 — the root — and the rule below generates $f_s$; hence $\mathcal{H}_k^0$ is *identically* distributed to $\{f_{U_k}\}$, the pseudorandom-function instance. At $i = k$ the random strings sit at level $k$, i.e., at the leaves, one independent uniform $k$-bit value per input: $\mathcal{H}_k^k$ is a truly random function. So the claim "$f_{U_k}$ is indistinguishable from a random function" is exactly "the extreme hybrids $\mathcal{H}_k^0$ and $\mathcal{H}_k^k$ are indistinguishable".

**Step 3 — distinguishing neighboring hybrids means distinguishing many samples.** Fix $i$ and suppose a PPT oracle machine $D$ distinguishes $\mathcal{H}_k^i$ from $\mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$ with gap $\delta(k)$. Build a distinguisher $D'$ that receives $m = 2^i$ strings $z_\sigma \in \{0,1\}^{2k}$ (indexed by $\sigma \in \{0,1\}^i$) and simulates $D$ with oracle access to the function obtained as follows: split each $z_\sigma = z_\sigma^0 z_\sigma^1$ into halves and **place the two halves at the two children of the level-$i$ vertex $\sigma$** (i.e., at the level-$(i+1)$ vertices $\sigma 0$ and $\sigma 1$); label everything below level $i+1$ by the deterministic GGM rule; answer each oracle query by walking down to the appropriate leaf. The crucial observation is that *below level $i+1$ the GGM rule is applied in both hybrids*, so the whole function — hence the complete view of $D$ — is determined by the $2^{i+1}$ level-$(i+1)$ labels alone. Now:

- if the samples $z_\sigma$ are drawn from $G(U_k)$: since $z_\sigma = G(r_\sigma) = G_0(r_\sigma) G_1(r_\sigma)$ for independent uniform $r_\sigma$, the two children of each level-$i$ vertex receive exactly the GGM-expanded labels of independent uniform level-$i$ strings — this is precisely the distribution of $\mathcal{H}_k^i$;
- if the samples $z_\sigma$ are drawn from $U_{2k}$: the $2^{i+1}$ level-$(i+1)$ labels are independent uniform — precisely the distribution of $\mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$.

Hence $D'$ distinguishes $m = 2^i$ independent samples of $G(U_k)$ from $m$ independent samples of $U_{2k}$ **with the same gap $\delta(k)$** — the reduction is lossless.

**Step 4 — many samples are as good as one (for polynomially many).** By the multiple-sample invariance of computational indistinguishability (Proposition 2.6: for polynomial-time constructible ensembles, indistinguishability by a single sample is equivalent to indistinguishability by $s(\cdot)$ samples for every polynomial $s$; proof by the hybrid technique of Module 3), and since $m = 2^i \le 2^k = \mathrm{poly}(k)$, pseudorandomness of $G$ implies that $m$ samples of $G(U_k)$ are indistinguishable from $m$ samples of $U_{2k}$. If $\delta(k)$ were non-negligible, $D'$ would violate this — contradiction.

**Step 5 — conclude by the hybrid chain.** Steps 3–4 show $\mathcal{H}_k^i \approx \mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$ for every $i = 0, \ldots, k-1$; chaining the $k+1$ hybrids (each step costing a factor $\mathrm{poly}(k)$ in the gap, which preserves negligibility) yields $\mathcal{H}_k^0 \approx \mathcal{H}_k^k$, i.e., $\{f_{U_k}\}$ is indistinguishable from a truly random function. ∎

**Why so many samples?** One might try to interpolate between $\mathcal{H}_k^i$ and $\mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$ vertex by vertex over the $2^i$ level-$i$ vertices, which would reduce to a *single* sample of $G(U_k)$ versus $U_{2k}$ — but the averaging would lose a factor $2^i$, which is exponential when $i$ is close to $k$. The Primer's route avoids this: it observes that the *entire* difference between the two hybrids lives in one layer of $2^i$ independent copies of $G$, i.e., in a batch of samples of size $2^i = \mathrm{poly}(k)$, and multiple-sample indistinguishability with polynomially many samples follows from the PRG property with only polynomial loss (Proposition 2.6). This is the standard template for "tree" constructions: isolate one level of independence and reduce to many samples of the underlying primitive.

## §2.8 Conceptual reflections, read through the GGM lens

The construction is a good excuse to revisit the conceptual reflections that close Chapter 2.

- **Behavioristic versus ontological.** The Kolmogorov–Chaitin approach declares a string random when it has no substantially shorter *explanation* than itself — an ontological stance about the "true nature" of the object. The computational approach cares only about the *effect* of objects on observers (what a feasible test can detect) — a behavioristic stance. The GGM function $f_s$ is the starkest example: its $2^k$-entry table is generated by a $k$-bit seed, so ontologically it is an extremely structured, compressible object; behavioristically it is indistinguishable from a uniformly random function. Even probability distributions that are not uniform — indeed not even statistically close to uniform — can be indistinguishable from uniform to all efficient devices, so objects that are ontologically very different are equivalent from the behavioristic viewpoint.
- **A relativistic, subjective view of randomness.** Pseudorandomness is defined *relative to a class of observers*. Here the observer class is PPT oracle machines (with an oracle and a single output bit); restricting the class (space-bounded observers, or very restricted ones that only run linear tests or hitting tests — Modules 7–8) yields different notions of pseudorandomness. The GGM tree looks random to polynomial-time observers only; an observer with unbounded power would trivially see the tree structure (the seed has only $k$ bits of entropy).
- **Randomness and computational difficulty are dual.** The whole paradigm rests on *difficulty*: distributions that are non-uniform yet indistinguishable exist only because distinguishing them is computationally hard. Each construction ingredient is a hardness assumption or fact: one-way functions give general-purpose PRGs (Theorem 2.14); later, hardness of parity for constant-depth circuits will generate sequences fooling such circuits (Chapter 3). GGM amplifies difficulty into a much richer object: the hardness of distinguishing one level of the tree becomes hardness of distinguishing the whole exponential collection of leaves.
- **Randomness and predictability.** Pseudorandomness is equivalent to unpredictability of the next bit (Yao; Modules 3–4), and the GGM proof is the tree version of the same intuition: each level of the tree is "unpredictable" given the levels above it, because predicting a level-$(i+1)$ label from the level-$i$ labels above it would mean distinguishing $G(U_k)$ from $U_{2k}$. The hybrid proof is exactly this unpredictability, unfolded level by level.

## Why this matters

- **Symmetric cryptography.** Pseudorandom functions are the workhorse of private-key cryptography: message-authentication codes (tag $v$ with $f_s(v)$), private-key encryption (mask $v$ with $f_s(v)$), and challenge–response identification all reduce to sharing one seed and evaluating $f_s$ locally — no communication, no synchronization, and values can be assigned online to arguments not known in advance.
- **Complexity theory.** PRFs are used to derive impossibility results in computational learning theory (some concept classes are not learnable if PRFs exist) and are the central object of the Natural Proofs framework, which shows that any "natural" proof separating complexity classes would yield a circuit distinguishing a PRF from a random function — hence natural proofs cannot work if strong PRFs (against small circuits) exist.
- **The arc of this course.** Definitions (Module 2) → the hybrid technique (Module 3) → concrete PRGs from hardness (Module 4) → here: a *generic* transformation showing pseudorandomness is closed under a huge jump in object size. The question that opens Module 6 — how strong a generator is needed to eliminate randomness in BPP — is precisely the §2.7.1 question of quantifying the distinguisher, and the answer will require flipping the paradigm: generators that may be slower than the distinguishers they fool.

defs.name: Pseudorandom functions (Definition 2.17)
defs.statement:
A collection of functions $\{f_s : \{0,1\}^{|s|} \to \{0,1\}^{|s|}\}_{s \in \{0,1\}^*}$ is a **pseudorandom function (ensemble)** if it satisfies:

1. **(Efficient evaluation)** There exists an efficient (deterministic) algorithm that, given a seed $s$ and an argument $x \in \{0,1\}^{|s|}$, returns $f_s(x)$.
2. **(Pseudorandomness)** For every probabilistic polynomial-time **oracle** machine $M$, every positive polynomial $p(\cdot)$, and all sufficiently large $k$:

$$|\Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k) = 1] - \Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k) = 1]| < \frac{1}{p(k)}$$

where $F_k$ denotes a uniformly selected function mapping $\{0,1\}^k$ to $\{0,1\}^k$ (equivalently: $2^k$ independent uniform $k$-bit values), and $M^g(1^k)$ means $M$ is run on input $1^k$ while making oracle queries to $g$ — it never receives an explicit description of $g$.
defs.intuition: A $k$-bit seed 'compresses' a table of $2^k$ entries into a tiny program: exponentially many pseudorandom values, each computable in polynomial time, with random access to any point. Parties that share only the seed share the same random-looking function, with no further communication.

defs.name: The GGM binary tree (labeling by PRG expansion)
defs.statement:
Let $G$ be a PRG of stretch factor 2, written $G(s) = G_0(s)G_1(s)$ with $|G_0(s)| = |G_1(s)| = |s|$ for every seed $s$. For a seed $s$ of length $k$, build a **full binary tree of depth $k$**:

- The root (the level-0 vertex) is labeled by the string $s$.
- If an internal vertex is labeled $r$, then its **left child is labeled $G_0(r)$** and its **right child is labeled $G_1(r)$**.

Every vertex at level $i$ carries a $k$-bit label (halves preserve length), and the leaves at level $k$ carry the outputs. For an input $x = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_k \in \{0,1\}^k$, the value $f_s(x)$ is the label of the leaf reached by starting at the root and, for $i = 1, \ldots, k$, descending to the left child if $x_i = 0$ and to the right child if $x_i = 1$. Equivalently, $f_s(x) = G_{x_k}(\cdots G_{x_2}(G_{x_1}(s))\cdots)$, where $G_{x_1}$ is applied first, at the root.
defs.intuition: The tree is the branching program of the function: the input bits steer a root-to-leaf walk, and the PRG generates the exponentially many labels on demand. Only the $k+1$ labels on the walked path are ever computed, which takes exactly $k$ evaluations of $G$.

defs.name: Strong generators: (T,F)-strong and non-uniformly strong (Definition 2.15)
defs.statement:
**((T,F)-strong generator, §2.7.1.)** Let $T$ be a class of time bounds and $F$ a class of (noticeable) functions, e.g., $T = \{t : t(k) = 2^{c\sqrt{k}}\}_{c}$ and $F = \{f : f(k) = 1/t(k),\; t \in T\}$. A pseudorandom generator $G$ with stretch $\ell$ is **$(T,F)$-strong** if for every probabilistic algorithm $D$ whose running time on a $k$-bit seed is bounded by some $t \in T$, for every $f \in F$, and for all sufficiently large $k$:

$$|\Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1] - \Pr[D(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1]| < f(k)$$

That is, the distinguisher's resources and the allowed success gap are quantified as functions of the **seed length $k$**.

**Non-uniformly strong PRG (Definition 2.15, §2.6).** A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm $G$ is a *non-uniformly strong pseudorandom generator* if there exists a stretch function $\ell$ such that for every family $\{C_k\}_{k}$ of polynomial-size circuits, every positive polynomial $p(\cdot)$, and all sufficiently large $k$:

$$|\Pr[C_k(G(U_k)) = 1] - \Pr[C_k(U_{\ell(k)}) = 1]| < \frac{1}{p(k)}$$

Such a generator satisfies the basic definition (Definition 2.1) and, moreover, fools all polynomial-size circuits rather than only probabilistic polynomial-time machines; indistinguishability by circuits is preserved under multiple samples regardless of the constructibility of the underlying ensembles.
defs.intuition: These strengthenings are what worst-case derandomization needs: the argument of Theorem 2.16 hard-wires each potentially bad input into a circuit, so the generator must fool non-uniform families of polynomial-size circuits, with resources measured in the seed length.

theorems.name: Theorem 2.18 (GGM: PRG ⇒ PRF)
theorems.statement: **Pseudorandom functions can be constructed using any pseudorandom generator.** Concretely, let $G$ be a PRG with stretch factor 2, $G(s) = G_0(s)G_1(s)$ with halves of length $|s|$, and let $f_s$ be defined by the GGM binary tree: $f_s(x_1 \cdots x_k) = G_{x_k}(\cdots G_{x_2}(G_{x_1}(s))\cdots)$, the label of the leaf reached from the root $s$ by taking the left child on bit 0 and the right child on bit 1 at each level. Then $\{f_s : \{0,1\}^{|s|} \to \{0,1\}^{|s|}\}_{s \in \{0,1\}^*}$ is a pseudorandom function ensemble: for a uniformly chosen seed $s \leftarrow U_k$, no probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine can distinguish oracle access to $f_s$ from oracle access to a truly random function $F : \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$.
theorems.intuition: One $k$-bit seed unfolds, along a depth-$k$ binary tree, into $2^k$ 'independent-looking' $k$-bit values, each computable with only $k$ PRG evaluations. The hybrid argument peels the tree level by level, and each peeling step is charged to the pseudorandomness of $G$.
theorems.proof:
**(Hybrid proof sketch, completed.)** Let $G$ have stretch factor 2 and write $G(s) = G_0(s)G_1(s)$.

*Construction.* For $x = x_1 \cdots x_k$ define $f_s(x_1 \cdots x_k) = G_{x_k}(\cdots G_{x_2}(G_{x_1}(s))\cdots)$ — i.e., walk a full binary tree of depth $k$ whose root (level 0) is labeled $s$ and in which a vertex labeled $r$ has left child $G_0(r)$ and right child $G_1(r)$; $f_s(x)$ is the label of the leaf reached via the bits of $x$. Every label has length $k$ (halves preserve length) and evaluating $f_s(x)$ costs exactly $k$ applications of $G$, so evaluation is efficient. The claim is that $\{f_{U_k}\}$ is indistinguishable from a uniformly random function.

*Hybrids.* For $i = 0, \ldots, k$, let $\mathcal{H}_k^i$ be the ensemble of functions $\{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$ obtained by placing $2^i$ independent uniform $k$-bit strings at the vertices of level $i$ (one per vertex $\sigma \in \{0,1\}^i$), and labeling every vertex **below** level $i$ by the deterministic GGM rule (left child $G_0(r)$, right child $G_1(r)$ of a node labeled $r$). For $x = \sigma\alpha$ with $|\sigma| = i$, the value is $G_{\alpha_{k-i}}(\cdots G_{\alpha_1}(s_\sigma)\cdots)$.

*Extremes.* At $i = 0$ the single random string sits at the root, so $\mathcal{H}_k^0$ is distributed exactly as $\{f_{U_k}\}$. At $i = k$ the random strings sit at the leaves — one independent uniform $k$-bit value per input — so $\mathcal{H}_k^k$ is a truly random function.

*Neighboring hybrids.* Fix $i < k$ and suppose an oracle machine $D$ distinguishes $\mathcal{H}_k^i$ from $\mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$ with gap $\delta(k)$. Build $D'$ that on input $m = 2^i$ strings $z_\sigma \in \{0,1\}^{2k}$ (indexed by level-$i$ vertices $\sigma$) splits each $z_\sigma = z_\sigma^0 z_\sigma^1$ into halves and places them at the two children of $\sigma$ — i.e., at the level-$(i+1)$ vertices $\sigma 0$ and $\sigma 1$ — then labels everything below level $i+1$ by the deterministic GGM rule and simulates $D$ with oracle access to the resulting function (answering a query $x$ by walking to its leaf). Below level $i+1$ the rule is identical in both hybrids, so the oracle view of $D$ is fully determined by the level-$(i+1)$ labels. If the samples come from $G(U_k)$, each pair of children under $\sigma$ is $(G_0(r_\sigma), G_1(r_\sigma))$ for an independent uniform $r_\sigma$ — exactly the level-$(i+1)$ layer of $\mathcal{H}_k^i$; if the samples come from $U_{2k}$, the $2^{i+1}$ labels are independent uniform — exactly the layer of $\mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$. Hence $D'$ distinguishes $m$ samples of $G(U_k)$ from $m$ samples of $U_{2k}$ with the same gap $\delta(k)$, losslessly.

*Multi-sample invariance.* Since $m = 2^i \le 2^k = \mathrm{poly}(k)$ and the ensembles are polynomial-time constructible, Proposition 2.6 (indistinguishability by one sample $\iff$ by polynomially many samples; the hybrid argument of Module 3) turns pseudorandomness of $G$ into indistinguishability of $m$ samples of $G(U_k)$ from $m$ samples of $U_{2k}$. If $\delta(k)$ were non-negligible, $D'$ would contradict this. Thus $\mathcal{H}_k^i \approx \mathcal{H}_k^{i+1}$ for every $i$.

*Conclusion.* Chaining the $k+1$ hybrids (polynomial loss per step, still negligible overall) gives $\mathcal{H}_k^0 \approx \mathcal{H}_k^k$: $\{f_{U_k}\}$ is indistinguishable from a truly random function, so the ensemble is pseudorandom. ∎

**Why many samples, not one:** interpolating vertex by vertex over the $2^i$ level-$i$ vertices would reduce to a *single* sample of $G(U_k)$ vs $U_{2k}$ but lose a factor $2^i$ in the averaging — exponential for $i$ near $k$. Instead one observes that all randomness difference between neighboring hybrids is confined to one layer of $2^i$ independent copies of $G$ — a batch of polynomially many samples — where Proposition 2.6 guarantees indistinguishability with only polynomial loss.

theorems.name: Theorem 2.16 (derandomization of BPP)
theorems.statement:
If non-uniformly strong pseudorandom generators exist (Definition 2.15), then for every $\varepsilon > 0$:

$$\mathrm{BPP} \subseteq \mathrm{Dtime}(t_\varepsilon), \qquad t_\varepsilon(n) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} 2^{n^\varepsilon}$$

Equivalently, $\mathrm{BPP} \subseteq \bigcap_{\varepsilon > 0} \mathrm{Dtime}(2^{n^\varepsilon})$. (The shorthand 'BPP ⊆ P' found in course notes is realized literally when the generator has exponential stretch, $\ell(k) = 2^{\Omega(k)}$, so seeds of length $O(\log n)$ suffice and scanning all seeds costs $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ — the Chapter 3 / Module 6 story.)
theorems.intuition: Replace the random tape of a BPP machine by $G(U_{n^\varepsilon})$ and enumerate all $2^{n^\varepsilon}$ seeds, taking the majority answer. The generator must fool non-uniform circuits because each 'bad' primary input is hard-wired into a circuit; non-uniformly strong PRGs are exactly the assumption that makes the worst-case (not merely average-case) argument go through.
theorems.proof: **(Sketch.)** For $S \in \mathrm{BPP}$ let $A$ be a probabilistic polynomial-time decision procedure for $S$, fix $\varepsilon > 0$, and let $G$ be a non-uniformly strong PRG stretching $n^\varepsilon$-bit seeds into $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-bit sequences (used by $A$ as its random tape on primary inputs of length $n$). Combining them yields $A' = A^G$. On any input $x$ where $A(x)$ and $A'(x)$ differ significantly, the circuit $C_x(r) = A(x; r)$ is a polynomial-size circuit distinguishing $G(U_{n^\varepsilon})$ from $U_{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ — contradicting Definition 2.15 — so such inputs exist only finitely often; absorbing them into $A'$ gives a randomized algorithm $A''$ for $S$ whose randomness complexity is $n^\varepsilon$ and whose error is negligible. Finally emulate $A''$ on each of the $2^{n^\varepsilon}$ possible seeds and rule by majority: the resulting deterministic algorithm runs in time $2^{n^\varepsilon} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(n) = 2^{n^{\varepsilon+o(1)}}$. Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, $S \in \bigcap_{\varepsilon>0} \mathrm{Dtime}(2^{n^\varepsilon})$. ∎

checkpoints.question: In the GGM construction with a stretch-2 PRG G and a seed s of length k, which description correctly states how fs(x) is evaluated for x = x1…xk ∈ {0,1}^k, and at what cost?

options.text: Start at the root labeled s; for i = 1,…,k, descend to the left child (label G0 of the current label) if x_i = 0 and to the right child (label G1) if x_i = 1; output the label of the leaf reached. Only the k+1 labels on the walked path are materialized, costing exactly k evaluations of G, so the total time is polynomial in k.
First compute the labels of all 2^{k+1}−1 vertices of the full tree (each with one PRG call), store them, and then read off the leaf reached by x; this costs 2^k evaluations of G.
Apply G once to the whole string x and read the answer from the output; the tree is only a visualization and costs O(1) PRG evaluations.
Walk the tree from the leaf back to the root: start at x and apply the inverse of G0 or G1, k times, to recover the label of the root; this shows evaluation needs the inverse of G and hence is hard.

checkpoints.explanation: The tree is a branching program: the bits of x steer a root-to-leaf walk, and each step from a vertex labeled r requires running G(r) once to obtain the two child labels G0(r) and G1(r) and keeping the appropriate half. Only the path is ever materialized — k edges, k evaluations of G — so fs(x) is computable in poly(k) time (never 2^k). G need not be invertible; the walk goes root-to-leaf.

checkpoints.question: Which statement correctly describes the i-th hybrid H^i_k in the proof of Theorem 2.18 and the reduction between neighboring hybrids?

options.text: H^i_k places 2^i independent uniform k-bit labels at the level-i vertices and labels all vertices below level i by the deterministic GGM rule. H^0_k is distributed exactly as {f_{U_k}} and H^k_k is a truly random function. Distinguishing H^i_k from H^{i+1}_k is shown equivalent to distinguishing 2^i independent samples of G(U_k) from 2^i independent samples of U_{2k}, by placing the two halves of each given sample at the two level-(i+1) children of the corresponding level-i vertex and expanding deterministically below.

H^i_k places random labels at all levels above level i and deterministic labels below; its two extremes are {f_{U_k}} and the all-zero function, and neighboring hybrids are indistinguishable by the stretch factor 2 alone.
H^i_k and H^{i+1}_k differ only in the label of the root; distinguishing them is therefore equivalent to distinguishing a single sample of G(U_k) from a single sample of U_{2k}, with no loss.
The hybrids are indexed from i = k down to i = 0, and the proof works by interpolating vertex by vertex over the 2^i vertices of level i, which loses only a negligible factor 2^i.

checkpoints.explanation: The extremes are exact: one random string at the root (i = 0) reproduces f_{U_k}, and random strings at the leaves (i = k) are a uniform random function. The whole difference between neighboring hybrids lives in one layer of 2^i independent copies of G (the 2^{i+1} level-(i+1) labels), which is why the reduction targets 2^i samples of G(U_k) vs U_{2k} — and not a single sample: a per-vertex interpolation would lose an exponential factor 2^i.

checkpoints.question: Why does the derandomization argument of Theorem 2.16 require a generator that fools polynomial-size circuits (a non-uniformly strong PRG, Definition 2.15) rather than merely all probabilistic polynomial-time distinguishers?

options.text: The argument isolates the inputs on which the randomized procedure A and its pseudorandom replacement A^G differ: each such input x is hard-wired into the circuit C_x(r) = A(x; r), so the resulting distinguishers form a non-uniform family of polynomial-size circuits indexed by input length, and the generator must fool every circuit in that family.
Circuits run much faster than probabilistic Turing machines, so fooling them is automatically harder and makes the derandomization theorem more impressive.
BPP machines are themselves Boolean circuits, so the only proofs that can be applied to them are circuit-based arguments.
Non-uniform circuits use no randomness of their own, which matches the deterministic algorithm A″ that enumerates all seeds; PPT distinguishers would need to be derandomized first.

checkpoints.explanation: The proof of Theorem 2.16 is worst-case: it must rule out divergence on every input, including inputs that are hard to find. For each diverging input x it builds the circuit C_x(r) = A(x; r) with x hard-wired, and asks this circuit to tell G(U) from U. Because we cannot enumerate the bad inputs inside a uniform machine, the guarantee must hold against the whole non-uniform family {C_x} — precisely the content of Definition 2.15. (Uniform PPT distinguishers would only give the average-case guarantee of Proposition 2.3.)

exercises.prompt: Write the GGM construction in full detail. Let G be a PRG with stretch factor 2 and write G(s) = G0(s)G1(s). (a) Define the full binary tree, its labeling rule, and the function fs(x) for x ∈ {0,1}^k; give the closed-form composition for fs(x). (b) Argue carefully that evaluating fs on an input of length d uses exactly d applications of G — hence O(d) PRG calls — and that fs is computable in polynomial time. (c) State how large the explicit truth table of a random function {0,1}^k → {0,1}^k is, and explain how the seed sidesteps writing it down.
exercises.hint: For (b): each step of the walk moves from a vertex labeled r to one of its children; obtaining the child label G_b(r) requires running G(r) once and keeping half the output. Count steps, not vertices: depth d means d edges, so d calls, each on a string of length k (labels never change length because halves preserve length). For (c): a function {0,1}^k → {0,1}^k has 2^k inputs, each mapped to a k-bit value.

exercises.prompt: Prove the reverse direction, PRF ⇒ PRG, and reflect on why PRF is the strictly stronger notion. Let {fs : {0,1}^{|s|} → {0,1}^{|s|}} be a pseudorandom function ensemble. Pick distinct fixed inputs a1, …, a_{ℓ(k)} ∈ {0,1}^k for a stretch function ℓ (e.g., ℓ(k) = 2k, using any 2k distinct k-bit strings) and define G(s) = fs(a1) ⋯ fs(a_{ℓ(k)}). Show G is a PRG. Why must the inputs be distinct, and where does the argument use the oracle-machine form of Definition 2.17? Then explain the sense in which PRFs are strictly stronger than PRGs even though existence of one is equivalent to existence of the other.
exercises.hint: Given a distinguisher D between G(U_k) and U_{kℓ(k)}, build an oracle machine M that queries its oracle h at a1,…,a_{ℓ(k)}, concatenates the answers, and runs D. Under h = f_s with s uniform the input to D is exactly G(U_k); under a random h the answers are independent uniform k-bit strings precisely because the a_i are distinct. For the 'strictly stronger' part: consider random access to exponentially many pseudorandom values versus a string you must generate in full.

exercises.prompt: In Definition 2.17 the distinguisher is a probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine that may query its oracle adaptively, yet it outputs only a single bit. Explain (a) what 'adaptive' means in this context, why the definition deliberately allows adaptivity, and why this only makes the notion stronger — give a concrete cryptographic setting where adaptivity is essential; and (b) why a single-bit final answer is not a real restriction on the adversary: argue that any multi-bit or non-binary distinguishing strategy can be converted into a 1-bit distinguisher with essentially the same advantage.
exercises.hint: (a) Adaptive = each query may depend on earlier answers; the machine in Definition 2.17 is an unrestricted PPT oracle machine, and non-adaptive strategies are a special case, so adaptivity cannot weaken the requirement. Think of chosen-message attacks on MACs. (b) Distinguishability is a hypothesis test between two worlds ('h = f_s' vs 'h = random'). Any acceptance rule or real-valued test collapses to the binary event 'output 1 iff the test accepts', and the advantage is by definition the gap in probability of a binary event; the real power of the adversary lies in its queries, not in the width of its final output.
